meta.description: Popularly a Yogi-ism, but the line is a 19th-century quip, in joke form by 1876. Berra denied it in 1989, then printed it in The Yogi Book (1998).
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Never answer an anonymous letter'?
meta.ogDescription: Not a Yogi original: the saying is in print from 1838 and as a joke by 1876. Berra denied it in 1989 and claimed it in 1998.

answer.label: Not originally Yogi Berra — a 19th-century quip
answer.authorDates: In print by 1838; joke form by 1876 · author unrecorded
answer.sourceLine: Quote Investigator traces the maxim back through the 1800s — a version appeared in an 1838 issue of Mechanics’ Magazine, an 1873 letter-writing manual, and as a joke in the Sioux County Herald of Orange City, Iowa in 1876, decades before Berra was born. Berra himself denied the line in Yogi: It Ain’t Over (1989), then included it in The Yogi Book (1998).

source.excerpt: It is a wise thing never to answer an anonymous letter until you have found out who wrote it.
trail: Quote Investigator ↗ assembles the pre-Berra citations — 1838, 1873 and the 1876 Iowa newspaper joke — and concludes that “this quip has a long history, and a version was in circulation by 1876.”
Wikiquote ↗ places the line in its Misattributed section, recording the denial in Yogi: It Ain’t Over (1989), p. 11 and the later embrace in The Yogi Book (1998).
Both books are real and datable: Open Library ↗ records Yogi: It Ain’t Over as Berra with Tom Horton, McGraw-Hill, 1989, and the 1998 Yogi Book ↗ as Workman Publishing, New York.

No transcript, broadcast, interview or contemporaneous report has been located in which Berra says the line — the only book bearing his name that carries it is the 1998 collection, published 122 years after the joke was already in print.
source.excerptNote: The 1876 Sioux County Herald humour-column version, as transcribed by Quote Investigator — the earliest form of the joke located to date, roughly half a century before Berra was born.

source.rightsNote: Rights here are genuinely unsettled, so we assert nothing. The idea is an anonymous 19th-century maxim whose 1838, 1873 and 1876 appearances are long out of copyright, but the exact five-word sentence as it circulates today is documented under Berra’s name in The Yogi Book (Workman Publishing, 1998), which is firmly in copyright. Because we cannot tie the precise modern wording to a specific pre-1931 printing, we do not claim public domain for it.

author.name: Yogi Berra
author.kicker: The man it gets pinned on
author.heading: Who was Yogi Berra?
author.bio: Lawrence Peter “Yogi” Berra (born St. Louis, 12 May 1925; died West Caldwell, New Jersey, 22 September 2015) caught 19 seasons in the majors, almost all for the New York Yankees, winning ten World Series rings as a player — more than anyone in baseball history — and entering the Hall of Fame in 1972. Off the field he became the most quotable man in America, and the most quote-magnetised: dozens of folk sayings and vaudeville one-liners drifted onto his name simply because they sounded like him. He knew it, and titled his 1998 collection The Yogi Book: “I Really Didn’t Say Everything I Said!”

cite.sourceCitation: Earliest documented in “Nubbins of Humor,” Sioux County Herald (Orange City, Iowa), 1876, as “It is a wise thing never to answer an anonymous letter until you have found out who wrote it”; cited in Garson O’Toole, “Quote Origin: Never Answer an Anonymous Letter,” Quote Investigator, 13 October 2013. The bare five-word form appears under Berra’s name in Yogi Berra, The Yogi Book: “I Really Didn’t Say Everything I Said!” (New York: Workman Publishing, 1998).

misattribution.heading: How it became a Yogi-ism
misattribution.intro: This is a textbook quote-magnet case: an old anonymous joke that sounds so much like Yogi Berra that it eventually became one — with Berra’s own late-life blessing.

items.why: Wikiquote ↗ lists it under Misattributed, noting that Berra “expressly denied this widespread attribution” in Yogi: It Ain’t Over (1989), p. 11, but later embraced it in The Yogi Book (1998).

items.scope: The claim that it starts with Berra
items.why: The saying was already circulating a century earlier: an 1838 Mechanics’ Magazine letter, an 1873 letter-writing manual and an 1876 Iowa newspaper humour column all carry it, per Quote Investigator ↗.

The 1876 newspaper version carries a second clause — “It is a wise thing never to answer an anonymous letter until you have found out who wrote it” — recorded by Quote Investigator ↗. The short form is what circulates under Berra’s name.

misattribution.truthLine: Best evidence: an anonymous 19th-century quip, in circulation by 1876, that Berra first disowned and then adopted — Quote Investigator ↗ concludes only that “this quip has a long history, and a version was in circulation by 1876.”

context.heading: Why this one sticks to Yogi
lead: The joke only works if you take it literally: you can’t answer a letter whose sender you don’t know. That collision of flat practicality and obvious impossibility is the exact shape of a Yogi-ism, which is why the line drifted onto Berra’s name and stayed there — even though its documented life in print begins in the 1830s and its joke form runs in an Iowa newspaper humour column in 1876.

Berra’s own position moved. In his 1989 autobiography he ruled the line out; by the 1998 Yogi Book it is printed under his name with a straight-faced defence — some letters, he notes, carry a return address but no signature. Quote Investigator’s summary is that he “has expressed uncertainness about the saying, but he now believes that he did say it in the past.”
detailsBody: 1838 — Mechanics’ Magazine, Museum, Register, Journal, and Gazette prints a reply beginning “It has been a rule with me never to answer an anonymous letter…” — the principle stated as ordinary etiquette, no joke intended.
1873 — a letter-writing manual, Analysis of Letter-Writing, advises that “You should never condescend to answer an anonymous letter…”

1876 — the Sioux County Herald of Orange City, Iowa runs the punchline version in a humour column: “It is a wise thing never to answer an anonymous letter until you have found out who wrote it.” All three citations are laid out by Quote Investigator ↗.
context.pull: He denied it in 1989 and claimed it in 1998. The saying itself was already more than a century old.
